1:
Keil and Delitzsch treats this chapter as foil for what follows, since the announcement of Zion's desolation, on account of the corruption of both civil rulers and spiritual leaders, sets off the prophecy of salvation that comes after. Gill takes it for a new discourse delivered at another time and to another people, addressed to Judah and Benjamin rather than the ten tribes, and not to heads of families only but to those in the highest posts, who had a great share in the national guilt; such men are not to be spared for their grandeur, though they are to be addressed respectfully. Calvin observes that the prophets did not set down all they had spoken but only the chief points, since all that survives of this book could have been delivered in half an hour, and yet from it we may learn what the prophet's manner of teaching was over forty years.

Henry takes the question as a demand for practice, since the knowledge of judgment is of no avail without the doing of it: their business was to administer justice impartially, and the Hebrew phrase for partiality is to know faces, so that they were to know judgment and the merits of every cause rather than the faces before them. He states the principle first, that princes and prophets who faithfully discharge their office are to be honoured above other men, but when they betray their trust should hear of their faults and be made to know that there is a God above them to whom they are accountable; and he notes that the prophet had the testimony of his conscience that he had not shrunk from his duty for fear of men.

The charge is read as an inversion of their office. Clarke keeps the figure of the flock running from the previous chapter: the chiefs, instead of defending the sheep and finding them pasture, are like wolves who tear the skin off them and the flesh from their bones; and he sets against them a saying from the life of Tiberius, that when governors of provinces urged an increase of the tributes the emperor answered that it is the property of a good shepherd to shear his sheep and not to skin them, a maxim many rulers do not seem to understand. Calvin cites the same answer, and presses the two verbs, since the good hated is benevolence and the evil loved is injury, so that the words might be rendered haters of benevolence and lovers of mischief. Wesley reads the hatred as reaching further, to the good done and to those who do it, and Gill the same way, that they could not endure the company of good men.

Calvin analyses the butchery into its steps. Under the similitude of butchers the prophet sets out their savage cruelty: they take off the skin, eat the flesh, and break the bones to pick out the marrow; and the figure of the pot follows the trade, since a man who throws meat into a caldron does not put in the whole ox but cuts it up. From this Calvin draws what God chiefly requires of those in power, that they abstain from injustice, being armed with power and therefore bound to be a law to themselves. A private man disposed to do harm is restrained by fear of the laws, but in princes there is greater boldness and greater ability to do wrong, which is the very reason they ought to observe more forbearance. On the cry that is not heard, Gill and Clarke agree that it comes too late, the enemy being already in the land and the oppressor having stopped his ears against the oppressed; Ellicott sets beside it the words of an older prophet, that when they spread forth their hands God will hide his eyes, their hands being full of blood.
5:
The charge against the prophets is laid to one cause. Calvin says the accusation is first of avarice, the prophet declaring he speaks at God's command so the indictment may carry more weight; the desire of gain had so possessed these men that they made no difference between true and false, and sought only to please for pay. God repeats the name of his people here, he notes, since the indignity was the greater for being done to them: had the Assyrians or the Egyptians been pillaged by their own princes it would have been more tolerable. Gill puts the fault as a failure of office, men whose business was to direct the people leading them into mistakes about religion and government.

The biting is explained from the clause after it. Ellicott takes the threat of war against those who put nothing into their mouths as fixing the sense of the earlier phrase, that they say peace to those who feed them; and the Hebrew word rendered bite, he notes, is properly used of serpents, of an adder in the path, and so suits their false and lying nature. Clarke reads it the same way: so long as they are well provided for they prophesy smooth things and cry peace, while against the true prophet who makes no provision for their appetites they sanctify a war, calling on all to put down a man who foretells the destruction of the temple.

The night threatened is not the loss of a gift they had. Gill is careful here, since these men were never sent of God and had no prophetic talents that could be taken away; the meaning is rather that such dark providences would come upon them that they would not have the face to pretend any longer to vision from God. He offers a rendering which makes the night come because of the visions. Calvin describes the punishment as a stripping of dignity, so that they should in vain claim the name they had abused; when profane men clothe themselves with dignified titles they pervert everything with impunity, and there is no remedy except that God pull off the mask. He reads the particle as making the darkness their wages: as the people were deceived by their fallacies, night is repaid for vision and darkness for divination. Clarke traces the same reversal in time: they prospered a while but were carried into captivity with the rest, so that the day which gives light and comfort to others became darkness to them.

The covering of the lips is the one real dispute here. Ellicott finds two things in it: the lepers, cut off from all communication with men, covered the upper lip, and so do these prophets, cut off from communion with God; it was also a sign of mourning, which is why a later prophet was told to astonish the people by leaving his lip uncovered when his wife died. Wesley takes it of mourners, so that these shall mourn and pine in their shame, and explains the silence by saying that what they had given out as God's answer now appears not to have been his. Calvin will have none of it: some think the practice of mourners is meant, he says, but the interpretation is frigid, and he has no doubt the prophet means that the mouths of these teachers would be stopped, comparing a later prophet who says that men who had gloried in the name shall cast away the mantle and no longer show themselves. He adds that the word for diviners is generally used in a bad sense and that for seers in a good, though here both denote pretenders. Gill and Clarke agree on what will silence them: the event will prove their prophecies false, and they will be found in the very captivity they had said would not come.
8:
The claim to power is read as an answer to the men just described. Gill insists it is no vaunt or arrogance, since the prophet only sets himself against men destitute of the Spirit, of sordid disposition and with nothing but selfish ends in view, and ascribes his own qualifications not to himself but to the Spirit of God. Henry hears a protest that justifies his plainness with the princes, since he durst not have made so bold with great men but that he was carried out to it by a prophetical impulse, and it was not he that said it but God by him. Set the two beside each other, Henry says, and there is no comparison: what is the chaff to the wheat, or painted fire to real fire? The false prophets never had courage to deal faithfully with the people but flattered them in their sins, and were full of shame when they lived to see themselves proved liars. Ellicott makes the same contrast, that Micah returns to his denunciation of sin in high places with the fearlessness of his namesake, setting himself against the prophets of the lying spirit and declaring both his commission and the equipment given with it.

The three words in the claim are taken separately by everyone who handles them. Clarke reads the first as heavenly energy occupying the whole soul, the second as a judgment enabling a man to discern between the precious and the vile, and the third as a prevalent power against which vice cannot prevail. Calvin gives the same three, identifying the first with the word used for power in the New Testament, the second with discernment, and the third, on another writer's authority, with an intrepid firmness of mind against all opposing evils. Wesley compresses them into courage and vivacity, the discerning of times and seasons and of right from wrong, and resolution. Calvin adds that some render the phrase as the Spirit of Jehovah in the genitive while others put the words in apposition with power, the particle before Spirit seeming here to be a preposition meaning by.

Calvin turns the verse into a lesson for a minority. Micah stands up alone, in a courageous spirit, against all the false teachers, and does so knowing that they were many and that they appealed to their number, according to their usual practice, as their shield. Such confidence is what all God's servants ought to possess, that they may not succumb to the empty boastings of men who subvert the whole order of the Church; and whenever God permits his truth to be corrupted by false teachers popular with the great and the multitude alike, this example should be remembered, lest we be discouraged and the invincible power of the Holy Spirit be weakened in our hearts.

The second summons is treated as the proof of the claim just made. Calvin says the prophet begins here to prove what he had stated, and calls it an actual demonstration, since he dreaded no worldly power but boldly addressed the princes and provoked their rage; he had not boasted of what he failed to confirm. Calvin also explains why the Spirit was named first: however much the wicked may rage, they become less ferocious when the name of God is introduced, so that the name serves as a sort of hidden chain upon them, and the prophet mentioned the Spirit to give his doctrine a freer course. Gill reads the summons as an instance of his boldness and impartiality, since he begins with the principal men of the land and charges them with their sins to their faces. Clarke notes only that the appeal is like the one at the opening of the chapter.
10:
Building the city with blood is understood of money, not only of murder. Gill offers the possible works, the repairing of the temple, the adorning of the palace, the raising of fine houses, and traces the money to its sources, sums taken from murderers, plunder wrung from the poor, and bribes to pervert justice. Ellicott states the same in a line, that they acquired money for splendid buildings by spoliation and robbery, not stopping short of murder, and compares a later prophet's charge against a king who built his city with the spoils of war. Calvin anticipates the objection that the men were not literally cruel: when I speak of blood, he has the prophet say, there is no reason to contend about a name, since all iniquity is blood before God, and if your houses were built by plunder your cruelty is proved, as though innocent men had been slain by your own hands. He adds that a judge corrupted by money becomes a thief, and one who extorts will also shed blood. Clarke turns the verse outward, saying he knows no text more applicable to those who have made fortunes by wrongs that affect the life of man, naming the slave trade, and following the metaphor to the point of saying that in such houses the timbers are the bones and the mortar the blood of the people bought and sold.

The three offices of the next verse are taken together. Ellicott states the pattern, that every function is carried out through bribery by judges, priests and prophets, while the men claim and count on the protection of God, relying for safety on the presence of the sacred buildings. Clarke distinguishes the fault, since the charge does not touch regular officers salaried for giving their whole time to the office, but those who take bribes and decide for whoever pays most; and on their confidence he answers his own question, that God has his temple, his ordinances and his people there, and will yet abandon all because all is polluted. Gill excepts the reigning king, too good a man to be included, and supposes the prophecy was delivered early in his reign while the officers of the previous wicked reign were still in place, and may itself have occasioned the reformation that followed. Calvin observes that the prophet arraigns the chief men alone, as though the blame of all the evils lodged with them, since although every order was corrupt the evils began with none but them.

The closing sentence is the most remembered thing in the book. Ellicott records why: a century later the elders of the land cited this very prophecy in defence of another prophet on trial for his life, asking whether the king of that day had put Micah to death, or had not rather feared the Lord, so that the threatened evil was repented of. Wesley notes the same quotation and its effect, that the king and his princes took it well and repented, so execution did not come in their days. Clarke supplies the custom from a Latin poet, who speaks of the wrathful soldier dragging the hostile plough over the walls of a conquered city as the mark of total overthrow, and reports that after the later destruction a plough was drawn over the courts of the temple, to signify it should never be rebuilt. Keil and Delitzsch distinguishes the two names against those who make them the site and the mass of houses, taking Zion for the part of the city that held the royal palace and Jerusalem for the rest. Calvin measures the severity by what is destroyed: that God should expose to reproach the holy city, the mount and his own temple shows nothing is less tolerable to him than the false confidence of hypocrites, who could not boast of being his people without aspersing him.
